During Malla period, there were 7 chowks naming:

1\. Nhuchhen chowk 2. Aagan Chowk

3\. Kisi Chowk 4. Sahapu Chowk

5\. Nhasal Chowk 6. Dafoswan Chowk

7\. Kumari Chowk
Krishna Mandir

The temple was built in 1637 by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla. A 3
storied stone structure, it was built in the local variety of Shikhara
style called Granthakuta. There are 21 pinnacles in the temple. Below
the pinnacles are 3 stories. The first floor holds the main shrine of
Lord Krishna with shrines of Radha and Rukmini at each side. The
second floor is dedicated to Lord Shiva and the third to Lokeshwor
(Avalokiteshwor). The first-floor stone pillar carvings narrate the
events of the Mahabharat, while on the second floor there are visual
carvings from Ramayana.
Bhimsen Temple

Bhimsen (Bhin: dya) temple was built by Srinivas Malla in 1682. It is
renowned for its three interconnected golden windows. Bhimsen is a
great personality in Mahabharat. He was known to be brave and strong.
In Newa, he is traditionally worshipped as a god of business and
trade.

Bishwanath Temple

The temple, dedicated to God Shiva, was built in 1627 during the reign
of Siddhi Narsingh Malla. The roof supports are decorated with erotic
carvings. The temple is guarded by two stone elephants in the front
entrance. On the other side of the temple is the sculpture of a bull.
A stone linga is enshrined inside the temple.
Taleju Bhawani Temple

The temple was built by Siddhi Narsingh Malla in 1640 and rebuilt
(restored) by Srinivas Malla in 1667 after a fire. Taleju Bhawani was
the personal deity of the Malla kings. It is a five-storey temple with
triple roofs.
Jagannarayan Temple

The two-storey brick Jagannarayan or Charnarayan Temple measuring
6.62\*6.63\*10.6m, built in 1566 is dedicated to Narayan (God Vishnu).
The temple, believed to be the oldest in durbar square, stands on a
brick plinth with large stone lions, above which are two guardian
figures. The roof struts are carved with erotic figures.
Hari Shankar Temple

This three-storey temple, enshrines the half Vishnu half Shiva Deity,
has roof struts carved with scenes of the tortures of the damned, a
strange change from the erotic scenes on the Jagannarayan. It was
built in 1704-05 by Rudramati, daughter of King Yognarendra Malla.
Taleju Bell

Diagonally opposite the Taleju temple in the palace complex, the large
bell, hanging between two stout pillars, was erected by King Vishnu
Malla in 1736. An earlier bell, erected in 1703, was moved to the Rato
Machhendranath Temple at that time. Petitioners could ring the bell to
alert the king to their grievances. Behind it is a lotus-shaped pool
locally known as Maharani Pukhu.
Chyasim Dewal (Krishna temple)

This attractive octagonal stone temple completes to the front line of
temples in the square. The stairway to the temple is guarded by two
stone lions. The temple was built by King Vishnu Malla in 1723.
Royal Palace and Patan Museum
Forming the completely eastern side of the Durbar Square is the Royal
Palace of Patan. Parts of the palace were built in the 14th century,
but the main construction was during the 17th and 18th centuries
by Siddhi Narsingh Malla, Srinivas Malla and Vishnu Malla. Now the
palace has been designated as Patan Museum displaying the ancient art,
architecture and daily life royal things.
Keshav Narayan Chowk
It is inside the Patan Museum, to the north of the Mul Chowk. Keshav
Narayan Temple is located at the center of this chowk.
Mul Chowk
It is the most famous, largest and central courtyard among the three
main chowks. Vidya temple is located at its center and Taleju temples
stand around the courtyard. The doorway to the shrine of Taleju, on
the southern side of the courtyard, is confined by the statue of the
river goddess Ganga, on a tortoise, and Jamuna, on a carved makura.
Sundari Chowk
It is to the south of the Mul Chowk. It is designed with a sunken tank
known as Tusha Hiti. The entrance is guarded by the stone statues of
Hanuman, Ganesh and Nara-singha. To the eastern side of the chowk lies
the Bhandarkhal garden and pool.

name: Rato Machhindranath, Tabahal Patan
description:
Location:
Continue south nearly 400m (5 minutes walk) from Patan Durbar Square
exists Rato Machhindranath Temple on the western side of the road at
Tabahal also known as Machhindra bahal.
Existence:
Standing in a large, spacious courtyard the 3 storey temple dates from
1673, although an earlier temple may have existed on the site since
1408.
Description:
The temple's 4 elaborately carved doorways are each guarded by lion
figures and at ground level on the four corners of the temple plinths
are reliefs of a curious yeti-like creature. A diverse collection of
animals (including peacocks, horses, bulls, lions, elephants and fish)
tops the pillars facing the northern side of the temple; they are the
Tibetan symbols for the months of the year. The metal roof is
supported by 20 struts on each of the first and second level, and 12
struts in upper level, each showing Avalokiteshwara standing above
figures being tortured in hell. Prayer wheels are set into the base of
the temple.
Historical and Religious Importance:
Rato Machhindranath locally known as 'Bungadyo', the god of rain and
plenty comes in a variety of incarnations. To Buddhists he is the
Tantric edition of Avalokiteshwara while to Hindus he is another
version of Shiva. Each year during the Rato Machhindranath
celebrations it is paraded around the town on a temple chariot. The
complex celebration moves the image from place to place over a period
of several weeks in the month of Baisakh (April/May), finally ending
at Jawalakhel where the chariot is disassembled. Occurring on a 12
year, cycle the procession continues out of Patan to the village of
Bungamati, 5 km to the south. At Bungamati, the god has another temple
where, since 1593, it has been the custom for the image to spend 6
months of each year. The chariot is returned to Patan for the other 6
months.

name: Hiranya Varna Mahabihar (Golden Temple), Kwabahal Patan
description:
Location:
Continue north-west nearly 400m (6 minutes walk) from Patan Durbar
Square exists Golden temple on the western side of the road at Kwa
Bahal.
Existence:
This unique Buddhist monastery was founded in the 12th century,
although the earliest record of its existence is 1409.
Description:
The three-storied temple gets its name from the gilded metal plates
that cover most of its frontage and it is one of the most beautiful in
Patan. Entry is via an ornate narrow stone doorway to the east, or a
wooden doorway to the west from one of the interlinked courtyards on
the north side of Nakabahil. Entering from the east, note the gaudy
lions and the 1886 signature of Krishnabir, the master stonemason who
sculpted the fine doorway with its frieze of Buddhist deities. The
second doorway leads to the main courtyard of the Golden Temple; shoes
and leather articles must be removed to enter the lower courtyard.
Two large brass elephant statues guard the doorway and the façade is
covered by a host of gleaming Buddhist figures. Inside the main shrine
is a beautiful statue of Shakyamuni. To the left of the courtyard is a
statue of Green Tara and in the right corner is a statue of the
Bodhisattva Vajrasattva wearing an impressive silver and gold cape.
Facing the main temple is a smaller shrine containing a 'self-arisen'
chaitya. The four corners of the courtyard have statues of 4
Lokeshvaras (Avalokiteshwara) and 4 monkeys, holding jackfruits. A
stairway leads to an upper-floor chapel dedicated to a white
eight-armed Avalokiteshwara, lined with Tibetan-style frescoes
including a wheel of life.
The main priest of the temple is a young boy under the age of 12, who
serves for 30 days before handing the job over to another young boy.

name: Kumbheshwara Temple
description:
Location:
Continue north nearly 500m (7 minutes walk) from north-west of Patan
Durbar Square exists Kumbheshwara temple on the eastern side of the
road at Kumbheshwor locally known as Konti.
Existence:
It is only one 5-storied temple of Patan and one of the 3
free-standing five storied temples of Kathmandu valley. It was
originally constructed as 2-storied shrine by King Jayasthiti Malla in
1392 and later, the additional 3 stories were given by King Srinivas
Malla during 17th century.
Description:
The temple is noted for its fine proportions and elegant woodworking
and there are numerous statues and other temples (dating from
Lichchhavi to Malla period) in the temple courtyard that includes
Mahadev, Ganesh, Bagalamukhi, Harati, Manakamana, Kedarnath,
Badrinath, etc. The temple is, however, dedicated to Shiva, as
indicated by the large Nandi bull. The temple platform has two ponds
whose water is said to come straight from the holy lake at
Gosainkunda, a long trek north of the valley. On the southern side of
the temple exist Bagalamukhi temple and Bhairav temple. In addition,
there are 2 waterspouts (dhungedhara) outside the complex.
Religious Importance:
Bagalamukhi is one of the famous Shakti Peeths of the Kathmandu valley
and is visited by large number of people especially on Thursdays.
Janai Poornima Mela (usually August full moon) is one of the major
festivals where devotees come to worship the embossed silver sheath
worn by the temples sacred linga, which is placed in a special
pavilion in the middle of the pond filled with water for mela in the
hub temple. And other various social and religious rituals and
ceremonies are periodically organized by the local people at the
temple complex.

name: Mahabouddha, Patan
description:
Location:
Continue south east nearly 500m (7 minutes walk) from south-west of
Patan Durbar Square exists Mahabouddha Temple on the western side of
the road at Mahabouddha, Sundhara.
Existence:
The construction of shikhara style temple often called 'the temple of
a thousand Buddhas' was initiated by priest Abhaya Raj of Patan around
1585. Although he died before the temple could be completed, his
descendants labored on the monument for generations, completing the
project by 1601. Its consecration was witnessed by Siva Simha Malla,
who conquered Patan in 1597.
Description:
Despite its height, the temple is not immediately visible because it
is tightly surrounded by other buildings. It is a shikhara style
temple, modelled on the original Mahabodhi temple at Bodhgaya, India.
The temple takes its name from the terracotta tiles with which it is
covered, each bearing an image of the Buddha. The temple was rebuilt
after the 1934 earthquake. Unfortunately, the rebuilders ended up with
a different looking temple, and had enough bricks and tiles left over
to construct a smaller shrine to Maya Devi, the Buddha's mother, in
the corner of the courtyard. The surroundings lanes are full of shops
selling high quality Patan-style metal statues.

name: Rudra Varna Mahabihar (Ukubahal)
description:
Location:
Continue north-east nearly 600m (8 minutes' walk) from Patan Durbar
Square exists Rudra Varna Mahabihar on the southern side of road at
Ukubahal next to Mahabouddha.
Existence:
The main Uku Bahal central courtyard was started by King Shivadev
(590-604) as one of five monasteries. Although began by King Shivadev
the religious community was later revamped by Rudra Dev so its name
got known as "Shivadev Samskarita Rudravarna Mahavihara". At the point
when it was established the religious community was situated in the
Wankulli locale. So, its name become regularly known as Wankulli
Bihar. Throughout the years this changed to Uku Bahal.
Description:
It is one of the best preserved and oldest of all Bahals of Patan. The
area around Rudra Varna Mahabihar contains 3 courtyards and each has
interesting and unique features. The outer courtyard is marked by an
impressive gate with two flag-bearing lion statues on top. These were
later addition in 1680. A large rectangular structure with two-storey
gilded roofs encloses a courtyard absolutely packed with interesting
bits and pieces. There are Lichchhavi style Chaitya, dorjes
(thunderbolts), bells, banners, peacocks, elephants, garudas, rampant
goats, kneeling devotees and a regal-looking statue of Rana Prime
minister Juddha Shumsher who gave cash for the fixes to the Bahal
after 1934 earthquake. In addition, the lions are particularly
curious-apart from regular Nepali ones, seated on pillars with one paw
raised in salute.
The courtyard at the back of Mahabihar is relatively modern and
actually belongs to the residents surrounding it. Nonetheless its
worth taking a walk around it and possibly admitting some of the
painted sculptures and stupa there.

name: Central Zoo, Jawalakhel
description:
Location:
Nepal's only zoo is situated at Jawalakhel in Patan nearly 1.8km
south-west from Patan Durbar Square.
Existence:
Established as a private zoo in 1932 by Late Rana Prime Minister
Juddha Shumsher, it came under the ownership of Government of Nepal
after the political changes of 1950, opened to the public in 1956 and
its management was handed over to National Trust for Nature
Conservation (NTNC) in December 1995.
Description:
The central zoo, with an area of about 6 hectares, provides shelter to
a total of 942 individual mammal in 109 species, including 15 of 38
endangered local species including Royal Bengal tigers and one-horned
rhinoceros, as well as many animals from around the world including
hippos, siamang, ostriches, chimpanzee, many birds, fish and reptiles.
There is a pond inside the zoo area which was built during the rule of
King Siddhi Narsingh Malla.
It serves as research, educational and recreational center for
visitors. The zoo includes a library, a children's small fun park,
picnic areas and paddle boats on the pond. Fishing is allowed in the
pond during some parts of the year. The zoo uniquely serves as a
historical cultural site for diverse groups of people.
The zoo opens 10:00 to 5:00pm hours from Sunday to Saturday. Visitors
need to purchase tickets and use of plastic bags is prohibited.

name: Ashokan Stupas, Patan
description:
Another remarkable feature of Patan is its 4 Ashoka Stupas that are
testimony to an ancient architectural tradition. The historians
believe that these stupas might have been erected in connection with
the foundation of Patan towards the end of the 4th century. Because
of its circular base and hemispherical dome, it can be said that these
have not been constructed in accordance with the Buddhist
architecture. It is said that Emperor Ashoka ever visited Kathmandu
valley and these stupas are supposedly built by him.
Lagan Thura-Southern Stupa
The southern mound is known as Lagankhel Stupa or Lagan Thura Stupa
located at Lagankhel. It is the largest among the 4, measuring 47.40m
in diameter and 11.80m in height. The mound is crowned by a recent
structure, a miniature cenotaph added on the top. The shrines of
Tathagatas were presumable added in 1878.
Teta Thura-Eastern Stupa
It is located about 200m east of Tyagal Tole near the eastern ring
road. The perimeter of this stupa is 75.83m and height 10.4m. It has
fire Vedica of height 1.6m with one Tathagata in each direction. The
dome of 4.5m in height is paved with firebricks. A square shaped
Harmika enshrines the dome.
Pucho Thura-Western Stupa
It is located just at the roadside of Pulchowk bus stand on the west
end of Patan. The perimeter of this stupa is 75.52m and height 12m. It
has firebrick Vedika of height 1.2m with one Tathagata in each
direction. The dome is 6.5m tall paved by firebrick. It has no
Harmika. The 13 rings Cakravalis are constructed directly over the
dome in square shaped pyramid structure.
Ibahi Thura-Northern Stupa
It is comparatively more complex and smaller one, located near
Shankhamul, northern side of Patan Durbar Square. This is similar in
structure of Swoyambhu Mahachaitya. It is nearly circular with
perimeter of 60.62m. It has 5 Buddha in the Vedika with their consorts
except the Tathagata. It has a Vedika of 1.5m and dome of 5.5m height.
A square Harmika is constructed over the dome with 13 steps Cakravali
and a parasol.

name: Godawari
description:
National Botanical Garden

 
Location:
The National Botanical Garden is located in the base of Mount
Phulchoki (2715m.) at Godawari (1515m.) at the 10km south east corner
of Patan.
Existence:
This garden was graciously inaugurated by His Majesty the King Late
Mahendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev on the 20th October 1962 (2019 B.S).
Description:
This botanical garden was designed by two British designers G.A.C.
Herklots and Tony Schilling. It is widely regarded as a center of
plant conservation, education, research and recreation. It spreads
over an area of 82 hectares of varying topography, among which, 40
hectares has been developed into various garden units. It is
surrounded by natural evergreen forests dominated by
Schima-Castanospsis and Alnus. It comprises a natural plant landscape
with various thematic gardens like a physic garden, biodiversity
education garden, rock garden, taxonomic family garden, fern garden,
special garden, Japanese style garden, VVIP plantation garden. A
natural stream (Godawari) is running from the mid garden. The garden
is the only one of its kind in the country boasting 4500 specimens of
flowering and non-flowering plants including large varieties of
orchids. The Godawari is home to at least 256 species of birds and
more than 300 species of butterflies and moths. This garden opens
daily from 9:00 am to 4:00 pm during the winter season and 9:00 am to
5:00 pm for the rest of the months.
Other places
Other places to visit in Godawari include Phulchoki Mai Temple,
Godawari Temple, Godawari Kunda, Bishankhu Narayan Temple, etc.
Phulchoki Mai temple is the three-tiered pagoda temple dedicated to
one of the Tantric mother goddesses and the two large pools are fed by
9 spouts (Naudhara) that represent the nine streams that flow down
from Phulchoki. Godawari Kunda is a spring where the sacred water of
the Godawari river pours down from the mountain and huge festival
takes place at Godawari temple once every 12 years in the autumn
season.

name: Bajrabarahi, Chapagaon
description:
Location:
The Bajrabarahi temple lies about 8 km south of Patan at a 30-minute
ride from the city. One of the 4 famous Barahi temples in Nepal,
Bajrabarahi temple is located at the meeting point of three Newar
settlements- Thecho, Chapagaon and Jharuwarasi.
Existence:
It is believed that the temple was built during the rule of Shree
Niwas Malla in 748 B.S. Before the temple was built, legend has it
that initially, there was a small pond where the temple lies today.
Description:
Embellished with ancient 17th century art, the temple is dedicated
to the tantric manifestations of Goddess Kali. The temple is
masterfully constructed in pagoda style, but lacks the most important
part of its design, the pinnacle (gajur), regarding whose absence
there are numerous myths. The raj pujari at Bajrabarahi says that he
has heard, since his childhood, stories about how the temple's
builders had been ordered to construct the structure in a single day.
And in a single day all structures were completed except pinnacle. It
is believed to be because of a priest's nightmare that depicted the
gory death of the workers if they ever tried to put on the gajur.
Because of the terrifying dream, there was a halt in the placing of
the gajur, which is put on last and ever since the temple has been
without one.
The inside of the temple features various incarnations of female
deities and the outside of the temple is guarded by two tiger statues,
the vehicles of Goddess Kali. In front of the main temple rests a
statue of bull, to whom devotees offer milk, ghee, curd and maize
flour every time their cattle deliver calves.
Over the course of the year, the temple hosts Jatra and festivals-one
that lasts 9 days during Navaratri, when worshippers pay homage to the
goddess Kali, Marasi Jatra and Purney Jatra during Kartik Purnima and
Chaitra Purnima respectively.

name: Nagdaha, Dhapakhel
description:
Location and Existence:
Nagdaha (Lake of Snakes), a mysterious lake is situated at about 5km
from Lagankhel, in a small village of Dhapakhel. The lake is believed
to be about 5 hectares and to have originated from a stone tap inside
Gaukhureshwor Temple, a temple on the north-western side of the lake.
Description:
The lake is known as a natural habitat for a variety of aquatic
plants, fish and migratory birds. The view of Phulchoki, Santaneshwor
and Kotadada can be seen from the lake.
One famous myth about this place is that a male serpent lives in
Taudaha and a female serpent is at Nagdaha. During the rainy season,
the male serpent makes a journey to the town of Panauti in order to
participate in a festival. It is said that he stays with the female
serpent of Nagdaha on his way to and back from Panauti. This union of
the nagas, mythical half serpent, half human beings, results in heavy
rain.
Nagdaha holds special religious significance. During Nag Panchami,
thousands of devotees visit the lake and take a dip in the pond and
perform puja in the temple. Rishi Panchami is also celebrated at
Nagdaha. In the Buddha Jayanti, monks from the nearby Bihars visit the
lake and release hundreds of fish into the lake signifying the
beginning of new life cycles.

name: Santaneshwor Mahadev, Jharuwarashi Badegaon
description:
Location:
It is one of the famous Hindu religious places located in the south
east of Kathmandu valley. It is situated at the border of Jharuwarasi
of Godawari municipality. Its height from the surface of sea level is
1400m and from the surface of land of its village is 100m. It takes
approximately a 1 hour drive (about 11km away) from Lagankhel.
Existence and description:
According to holy book, Lord Shiva lost his beloved wife. As he can't
tolerate the death of her and carry her dead body everywhere he goes,
thinking it to be alive. The other gods send the flies with their
supernatural powers to decay the body. As it is believed that the
upper lip had fallen in the top of the hill, where Santaneshwor
Mahadev is located today. Thus the name of the temple was given a name
Santaneshwor, which means a boon having a baby. On special occasions
such as 'Ekadashi', 'Maha Shivaratri', 'Teej' and 'Dashain', the
temple becomes a hive of activity, with huge numbers of hindu
followers gathering to worship.

name: Karya Vinayak
description:
Location:
Karyavinayak Temple is one of the four famous Vinayakas (Ganesh) of
Kathmandu valley, located in Bungamati, Lalitpur. It is about 10km
south of Kathmandu.
Existence and description:
The temple was dedicated on the fourth Thursday of the month of
Chaitra in Nepal Sambat 781 (1661 A.D.) under the leadership of local
leader Purna Singh of Bungamati. At this time the reign of Shri Niwas
Malla had just begun in Patan. Later, the temple was renovated during
the reign of King Mahendra. Worship originally took place on a
naturally formed stone in the shape of the deity, Ganesha, now a
statue of GAnesha covered with artistic silver, is kept inside the
temple.
Before starting any work, devotees come to Karyabinayak to wish for
the successful completion of that work. On the day of Pahan Chahre
(during the Ghode Jatra), there is a Karyabinayak deity procession in
Bungamati, at a place the people of Bungamati call "Gale", which means
forest. It is also a famous picnic spot.

name: Sikali, Khokana
description:
Location:
Sikali temple lies in the southern part of Kathmandu valley at an
approximate distance of 10km. The temple is located in an isolated
place, outside of the main settlements, but the surrounding is
heavenly. Paddy fields near the temple, flowing Bagmati river and the
view of Chandragiri and Champadevi hills makes the moment
unbelievable.
Existence and Description:
Sikali Mai temple is a huge three storey temple, where goddess
Rudrayani is worshipped and is considered as the protector of the
locals and localities. The temple was constructed during the reign of
Amar Malla during 1570 B.S. (1513 A.D.). During the time of Dashain
festival, local people of Khokana celebrate a 5 day long Sikali jatra
as an alternative to Dashain of the locals. The festival is found to
be celebrated since 336 Nepal Sambat, during the reign of King Amar
Malla. The festival beings from the day of Ghatasthapana. During the
festival, a wooden chariot carrying the idol of goddess Rudrayani, is
carried through the village streets, which is finally rested in front
of Sikali Temple. On the final day, a local dresses as Goddess
Rudrayani and comes out to battle against the devils.

name: Rato Machhindranath, Bungamati
description:
Bungamati is a Newar town on a spur of land overlooking the Bagmati
River. The central ritual focus of Bungamati is the Temple of
Machchhindranath. Locally known as 'Bungadyo' or 'Karunamaya', is the
temple for Rato Machchhindranath where the deity resides for 6 months
after returning from chariot procession of Patan.

name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square
description:
Location & Existence:
Bhaktapur Durbar Square, listed in UNESCO world heritage site, is a
former royal palace complex. It housed the Malla kings of Nepal from
12th century to 1428 and Malla Kings of Kingdom of Bhaktapur from 1428
to late 18th century until the kingdom was conquered to modern
Nepal. Most of the current architecture is from 1600s constructed
during the reign of malla kings that include Jagjyoti Malla, Jitamitra
Malla, Bhupatindra Malla and Ranajit Malla.
Descriptions:
Durbar Square is the vicinity of many temples and courtyards that
include:

1. Char Dham (Rameshvara, Badrinath, Kedarnath-Gopinath, Jagannath)

2. Nhekanjhya Layeku

3. Lun Dhwakha (Golden Gate)

4. Nge nyapa jhya layeku (55 jhyale durbar)

5. Vatsala Temples (Nritya Vatsala, Siddhi Vatsala, Yantra Vatsala,
 Annapurna Vatsala)

6. Statue of Bhupatindra Malla

7. Taleju Bell

8. Chyasilin Mandapa

9. Yaksheswara Temple

10. Silu Mahadev Temple

11. Yeti Chapari & Tava Sattal

12. Basantapur Durbar of Bhaktapur

13. Chaukota Durbar

14. Ganga Rani's Narayana Temple

15. Vatsala Falcha

16. Lapan Dega

17. Purveswara Mahadev Temple

18. Thanthu Layeku Durbar
Char Dham
 
The replica of the Char Dham of India was commissioned by Yaksha Malla
in 1451 A.D with the intention of giving old, weak and handicapped
citizens the satisfaction of worship the Char Dham without having to
go on a pilgrimage to these sites. The temples within the Char Dham at
the western side of the square includes domed temple of Rameswaram,
Gopinath Krishna temple (Dwarkadhish temple), terracotta temple of
Badrinath, Kedarnath and Nepalese pagoda styled temple of Jagannath.
The first temple on the right side as we enter the western gate is
Rameshwar temple, which is a Gumbaja style temple. It is an open
shrine with four pillars and it is dedicated to Shiva.
In 1667, the Gopinath Krishna temple was constructed in the Nepalese
two roofed pagoda style which replaces Kedarnath as one of the Char
Dham in Indian traditions. It is the temple attached to Rameshwara
temple houses three deities Balaram, Subhadra and Krishna. Also known
as the Krishna temple, houses three deities, left to right,
respectively: Satyabhama, Krishna and Radha. Their images are carved
in stone.
The Badrinath and Kedarnath sikhara style temples that stand on the
plaza. The present temple is a recent reconstruction that approximates
the original form of the temple, which was built by Bhupatindra Malla.
Badrinath is dedicated to Vishnu and Narayan whereas Kedarnath is
dedicated to Shiva.
The current Jagannath temple seems quite ordinary covered with a tin
roof. This one-storey temple was three times bigger and of two-storey
on its erection before the earthquake of 1934 A.D.
Nhekanjhya Lyaku Palace

The name of this palace is derived from a lattice window which had a
glass pane placed in it. The window, which has been lost today was
placed by Bhupatindra Malla with the intention of exhibiting a glass
pane which he had received as a gift from a Mughal emperor. The palace
is also known by other names such as Simhadhwaka Lyaku, named after
the two large statues of guadian lions and Malaticuka Lyaku after the
name of the courtyard north of the palace.
It was the main residence of the royals of Bhaktapur. The construction
of the palace was completed in 1698 (Nepal Sambat 818) during the
reign of Bhupatindra Malla. The current façade of the palace dates
from 1856 when the eastern part of the palace was demolished by Dhir
Shumsher Rana, who after a trip to Britain, commissioned a British
style building named 'Lal Baithak' in its place. The western half of
the palace was also altered to some degree in 1856, as although the
interiors were built in a British style, the outer façade still
retained some of the old Newar windows including the old palace's
namesake lattice window. The window has often been dubbed as the first
use of glass pane on a window in Nepal.
Behind the palace is a courtyard named, Malati chuka which is one of
the few remaining of the 99 courtyards of the royal palace. The
courtyard once housed a golden water spout as well but it has been
stolen. This hiti was also placed by Bhupatindra Malla along with gilt
copper statues of Hindu deities. He also built a single-storey temple
with a gold-plated rooof in the courtyard which was destroyed in the
earthquake of 1934 and was not reconstructed. In the present time, the
palace is used as national art museum.
Golden Gate (Lun Dhwaka)
The Lun Dhwaka, meaning 'golden gate' which serves as an entrance to
the inner courtyards of the former royal palace was constructed
between 1751 and 1754 by Subhakara, Karuunkara and Ratikara. The
project was initially planned in 1646 by Jagajjyoti Malla but the
goldsmiths only made model and died. So the work was finished during
the reign of Ranajit Malla in 1754. The gate serves as an entrance to
the shrine of Taleju, who was the tutelary goddess of the Mallas.
55 Windows Palace

The so called "Palace of 55 windows", a name derived from the local
term 'Nge Nyapa Jhya Lyaku' is the only palace in the square, whose
façade has been altered the least since its completion in 1708. It is
located on the north side of the square and comprises the Tripura
palaces's southeast wing. While the palace as a whole was founded in
the mid-12th century during the reign of Anandadeva, the 55 windows
wing was begun much later, in 1697, during the reign of Bhupatindra
Malla. It is a three-storey structure with two brickwork levels
interspersed with a rhythmic series of alternating doors and windows.
The upper level is constructed as a continuous balcony of 55 windows
with latticed screens, colonettes, and trilobate arches all made of
wood. The palace was built for musical purposes as indicated by 147
miniature carvings of musical raga on the cornice separating the
ground floor from the first.
Vatsala Temples
There are 5 temples dedicated to different forms of the mother goddess
Vatsala, meaning 'loving mother'. Among which 4 (Nritya Vatsala,
Siddhi Vatsala, Yantra Vatsala and Annapurna Vatsala) are in the
durbar square. The goddess Vatsala is locally believed to shield the
city from an epidemic and hence these temples were constructed with
the intention of prreventing one.
 
Nritya Vatsala Devi Temple
The Vatsala Durga, also known as Vatsala Devi or Nritya Vatsala, is
located on the east side of the square, sandwiched between the
Pashupatinath temple to the south and 55 windows palace to the north.
It is a sikhara-style monument, somehow similar to Krishna Mandir of
Patan, dedicated to the Vatsala manifestation of the female deity
Durga. Though the date of original construction is believed in 1690s,
the present form of the temple was built during the reign of King
Bhupatindra Malla (1696-1722).
Siddhi Laxmi Vatsala Temple
The temple of Siddhi Vatsala is a shikhar- style stone temple
dedicated to Siddhi Laxmi goddess. The original temple was built
during the reign of King Jitamitra Malla. It is located in east side
of the 55 windows palace. The temple is especially noted for its
guardian statues, which includes a man and a woman holding a child and
a chained dog, a pair of camels, horses, rhinos and mythical beasts.
Yantra Vatsala Temple
Yantra Vatsala, sister temple of Siddhi Vatsala temple, before being
destroyed in 1934 earthquake, used to exist north of it. It was not
restored after that earthquake, and instead a one storey building has
been constructed in order to shelter the image of the deity.
Annapurna Vatsala Temple
It is located south of the Yakshasvara temple is more commonly known
as 'Guheshwori of Bhaktapur'. The image of the deity the small shrine
is similar to the Annapurna temple located in Asan, Kathmandu. It is
rather small when compared to its sister temple, it is unknown whether
it is a reduced structure as restoration after the 1934 earthquake.
Statue of Bhupatindra Malla
A gold plated bronze statue of Bhupatindra Malla, who ruled Bhaktapur
from 1696 to 1722 is placed in stone column at the center of the
square. The statue has a bullet hole in its leg from 1769, a remnant
of the Battle of Bhaktapur.
Taleju Bell
The Taleju Bell, 'tava gan' is a large bell dedicated to Taleju
goddess, offered by the last monarch of the city, Ranajit Malla on 6
January 1737. The construction of the bell started on June 1732 and
took 4 years and 6 months to complete. The bell was rung once everyday
during the pooja of the goddess. It is the oldest one among other
similar bells of Kathmandu and Patan.
Chyasilin Mandap

Chyasilin Mandapa, translating to 'octagonal pavillion' from Newar,
was a two storey structure that existed south of the palace of 55
windows. In local folklore, it is attributed to Bhupatindra Malla who
is believed to have commissioned the building to protect his
residence, the palace from the harmful energy radiated by the lingam
housed in the nearby Yaskhavara temple which pointed north towards his
residence. In actuality, however, the Chyasilin Mandapa was
commissioned by Srinivas Malla of Lalitpur who erected this building
as a sign of friendship between him and Jagat Prakash Malla of
Bhaktapur. It was also used by the monarchs to meet the ambassadors
and other officials, by the court to watch the festival procession.
Yakshasvara Temple

The Yakshasvara temple is foten called the 'Pashupati of Bhaktapur'
becasuse of the architectural similarities with the Pashupatinath
Temple in Kathmandu. The temple was constructed by Karpura Devi in
1484 and was dedicated to her deceased husband, Yaksha Malla. Housed
inside is a lingam similar to that of the Pashupatinath temple in
Kathmandu. This temple is also noted for its erotic wooden carvings.
Silu Mahadeva

It was the tallest temple of the square; a terracotta temple that
stood on a pedestal containing sculptures of its guardians, namely
lions, elephants and cows. The temple enshrined a lingam associated
with Silu, a lake in northern Nepal that is considered sacred to
Shiva, hence it is named as Silu Mahadeva. The temple, based on its
architecture is thought to be from the 17th century or earlier but
its exact antiquity is not known yet. The temple was destroyed in the
1934 earthquake and replaced with a small dome like structure known as
'Phasi dega' during its restoration. Later the temple was restored to
its original pre-form in 2022 A.D after 2015 earthqauke.
Yetachapari and Tava Sattal
 
These two structures are colloquially referred as taha falcha, a
falcha being a communal resting place common in Nepal. Yetachapari
located on the central part of the square whereas its sister
structure, Tava Sattal is located on the eastern part of the square.
Lost Heritages of Bhaktapur Durbar Square
Basantapur palace of Bhaktapur
The most important building of the western part of the square was the
'Basantapura rajakula', formerly a nine-storey palace. The palace was
also called 'nakachhe tavagola kwatha' means 'a large fort meant for
festivals'. The building was originally commissioned by King Jagat
Prakash Malla in 17th century but was damaged in 1681 earthquake.
His grandson, Bhupatindra Malla had it repaired in May 1702 when he
also inagurated the sculptures of Ugrachandi and Ugrabhairava placed
near the entrance of the palace. The palace was once covered a large
area and was the largest and tallest palace of Nepal before being
partially destroyed in 1833 earthquake and was demolished by Dhir
Shumsher Rana who established a kitchen garden in its area. Later in
1947, a government school awas shifted to the area which still stands
there. Excavation work has not been done, today the only remaining
part of the palace are the 2 large statues of guardian lions and pair
of statue of Ugrachandi and Ugrabhairava.
Chaukota Palace
Not much is known about this palace, which once existed east of the
Basantapura palace. The palace was likely demolished during the
restoration work commissioned in 1856 by Dhir Shumsher Rana. This
palace is mentioned in an inscription during the reign of Jitamitra
Malla (1672-1696), so it must date from before his reign. Similarly,
during the battle of Bhaktapur, it is said that Ranajit Malla took
shelter in this palace as the invading Gorkhali armies started to
enter the square. The word 'Chaukota' literally means 'four forts' and
as such the palace seems to have functioned as a fort.
Ganga Rani's Narayana Temple
The extinct Narayana temple built as a small two storey pagoda was
commissioned by Ganga Rani and was located on the immediate south of
the western corner of te Nhekanjhya Lyaku. Ganga Rani was a queen
regnant of Bhaktapur who jointly ruled the kungdom with her sons from
1559. The temple was likely demolished in 1856 by Dhir Shumsher Rana.

Vatsala Falcha
Vatsala Falcha was a small falcha or a communal resting place that was
located on the southern part of the square, just south of the
Yakshasvara temple. It was destroyed in the 1988 earthquake but the
plinth in which the falcha stood still exists today.
Lapan Dega
Lapan Dega, which means 'temple that blocks the path' was the tallest
Nepalese pagoda style temple of the square. It was erected by Srinivas
Malla of lalitpur in 1657 as a sign of friendship between him and
Jagat Prakash Malla of Bhaktapur. The temple was constructed right on
the traditional path that festive processions took while passing
through the square, hence the temple was given the name Lapan Dega
meaning 'temple that blocks a path'. The temple was architecturally
very similar to the Nyatapole. The temple was destroyed in the 1934
earthquake and was subsequently never restored. Now, only the stone
guardian lions stood in their original place.

Purvesvara Mahadeva Temple
This temple was also known as
Mashanesvara Mahadev temple and was another lost temple located in the
eastern part of the square behind the large falcha, 'tava falcha'. The
lingam enshirined in this temple pointed eastwards instead of the
usual north, hence the temple is referred as Purvesvara or the eastern
land. Built in Nepalese pagoda style, this temple was destroyed in the
1934 earthquake and never get restored.
Thanthu Lyaku Palace
Translateing to 'upper palace' from newar, Thantu Layaku occupied an
extensive area containing numerous buildings, courtyards and gardens.
An inscription set up by the 17th century king Jitamitra Malla, is
currently the only surviving physical description of the palace
complex. Based on the inscription, the palace can be dated to around
19 June 1678. During the Rana regime, its gardens were turned into
government offices and the main palace was remodelled as Rana style
building. The few surviving parts of the palace were destroyed in 1934
earthquake and has been replaced with commercial buildings and
school.Today, only a single courtyard of the palace containing a
golden fountain survives and the remodelled wing of the palace is
currently restored to its former Malla dynasty look after 2015
earthquake.

name: Nyatapola Temple
description:
Locally known as 'Nyatapau' in newari meaning 5 storey roof, nyatapole
is one of only two five-tiered pagodas in the whole of the Kathmandu.
It stands at the north end of Bhaktapur's Taumadhi square. This temple
was commissioned by King Bhupatindra Malla from December 1701 to July
1702. The temple's sanctum enshrines Bhagawati in her specific
incarnation as either Siddhi Laxmi or Taleju, a deity worshipped by
the Malla kings as a protectress of the kingdom.
There are five plinths on the stairways to the entrance of the temple
and each of the plinth has a pair of stone guardians. Each of the pair
is said to 10 times stronger than the one below them. At the bottom
are two Rajput wrestlers named Jai and Pratap who are said to be 10
times stronger than the normal men. Above them are the giant statues
of two elephants and above them are the statues of two Singhas, which
is a mythical big cat. Above the cats are the statues of two Sardulas,
a griffin-like creature of local newari mythology. And in the topmost
plinths are the Tantric deities, Simhani and Vyaghrani, the lioness
and tigress deity who are the strongest of all the guardians. There
are also a total of 5 Ganesha idols on 4 shrines, one on each corner
of the structure.

name: Bhairavnath Temple
description:
The Bhairavnath temple stands on the east side of Bhaktapur's Taumadhi
square, southeast of the main durbar square. Also known as the Kashi
Bishwanath or the Pantali Mandir, it is a three-storey, rectangular
temple dedicated to the god Bhairav (Naso Dyo), an incarnation of
Shiva. The temple was first built during the reign of King Jagjjyoti
Malla (1614 to 37) as a much smaller one-storey structure. The second
tier was added by Bhupatindra Malla in 1717. The final tier was added
either by Malla or was constructed following the devastating 1934
earthquake. Curiously, there is no entrance on the temple's lengthy
west façade that faces the square. Instead, priests access the
interior from the south. The west façade is largely symmetrical and
features a ground-level shrine with Bhairav depicted in miniature on a
small metal throne.

name: Dattatreya Temple
description:
The Dattatreya temple stands at the east end of the Tachapal tole, a
small square on the east side of Bhaktapur. It honors the cmposite
deity Dattatreya, a personification of the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu
and Shiva. The temple was originally founded as a sattal, a kind of
dharmashala sometime in the 15th century. It was functionally
similar to the Kasthamandapa of Kathmandu, supposedly using the timber
from a single tree. The Dattatreya was probably erected between
1428-67, either by Yaksha Malla, or possibly by his son Raya Malla. At
some later date, probably during the reign of Vishva Malla (1547-60)
or Jitamitra Malla (1663-96), the design was altered to change the
sattal into that of a temple for worshipping Dattatreya. The
three-storey temple is raised above the ground on a brick and
terracotta base, which is carved with erotic scenes. The main steps to
the temple are guarded by statues of the same two Malla wrestlers who
watch over the first plinth of the Nyatapola temple.

name: Siddha Pokhari
description:
Siddha Pokhari is located near the main entance to Bhaktapur Durbar
Square and is among the older ponds in Bhaktapur. This is considered
to be the oldest pond in Bhaktapur. It holds an area of 275m\*92m and
is rectangular. Naturally, a pond this big would have a lot of fish
living in it. Along with the fish, there is also a Shiva Linga roughly
around the center point of this pond. Also known as Indra Daha, this
pond is related to the goddess Indrayani. The path is paved with a
classic brick city layout.
Regarding its origin, there are different views according to hisorical
documents. One theory suggests that Siddha Pokhari is a natural pond
that dates back to the Lichchhavi period. It has been here since at
least 250 A.D or 1700 years. The mere existence of Shiva Linga seems
to provide additional validity to that claim. Another theory suggests
Siddha Pokhari was made during the early 13th century during the
rule of King Ari Malla and was further developed during the rule of
King Jayayakshya or Yakhsha Malla of Bhaktapur.
Siddha Pokhari is still known as Ta: Pukhu, means big pond. After
unification , General Bhimsen Thapa renamed it as Siddha Pokhari,
carrying the essence of the Indra Daha.

name: Rani Pokhari
description:
Rani Pokhari of Bhaktapur is located near west of Siddha Pokhari. It
is said to be 40 years older than the Ranipokhari of Kathmandu. As per
historian, the Ranipokhari of Bhaktapur was ordered to be built by
King Jagat Jyoti Malla of Bhaktapur. It is assumed that he ordered the
building of the pond in remembrance of his wife, Queen Rajlaxmi. The
found inscriptions state that it was built in 1687 B.S. Later it was
renovated by King Jitamitra Malla in 1735. During the renovation,
several statues of gods and goddessess were believed to be installed
there.
It is said that there used to be a snake statue in the middle of the
pond. Beside historical importance, the Prajapati, Awal,
Jochhen,Maharjan, Bhujitu, Rajlawat people of Bhaktapur do their digu
puja at the premises of Ranipokhari.

name: Changu Narayan, Bhaktapur
description:
Location:
Changu Narayan temple is an ancient hindu and Buddhist temple, located
on a hilltop Changu (also known as Dolagiri) in Changu Narayan
municipality of Bhaktapur district of Nepal. It is about 7 miles
(12km) east of Kathmandu, and a few miles north of Bhaktapur.
Existence:
Though the main temple is said to be constructed by Lichchavi king
Haridutta Verma in 323 A.D, the temple houses the oldest inscription
of Nepal erected during the rule of King Mandev at around 464 AD. The
temple was recognized as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1979.
Description:
Changu Narayan is also known as Champak Narayan, Garud Narayan. The
temple was surrounded by champak tree forest and a small village known
as Changu. A Kashmiri king is said to have given his daughter,
Champak, in marriage to the prince of Bhaktapur. The temple is
considered to be named after her. The temple is dedicated to Lord
Vishnu.
The temple has traditional Nepali architecture, follows a pagoda-style
roof design with two levels, each with symmetrical pitched roofs.
There are four entrances to the temple and these gates are guarded by
life-size pairs of animals such as lions, mythic sarabhas, griffins
and elephants on each side of the entrances. The ten incarnations of
Lord Vishnu and the other idols are carved in the struts, which
support the roof.
There are other monuments in the temple surroundings after entering
from the main entrance (eastern gate) to the courtyard. Those include
historical pillar erected by Mandeva, Garuda, Chanda Narayan (Garuda
Narayan), Sridhar Vishnu, Vaikuntha Vishnu, Chhinnamasta, Vishworup,
Vishnu Vikrant, Narasimha, Kileshwor, etc.

name: Surya Vinayak, Bhaktapur
description:
Location & Existence:
Suryabinayak temple is a famous temple of Lord Ganesh. It is one of
the four major Ganesh shrines in the Kathmandu valley. It is located
2km south of Bhaktapur city in Sipadol VDC. The temple is believed to
have been originally built over 1500 years ago in the time of the
Lichchhavi King Vishnu Dev Barma.
Description:
The temple lies in the lush green hills, therefore famous as a tourist
and picnic spot. The temple, built of bricks, is built in the Shikhar
style. The temple looks beautiful due to the metal serpents extending
from the top of the white pillar in all directions. The construction
of the temple is clear from the inscription that it was completed on
the 7th day of Paush shukla saptami of 1890 B.S. Inside the temple,
there is a stone-shaped idol of Ganesh. There is a temple of the
goddess on the hill a little above the Suryavinayak. It is believed
that some speechless children can speak after being given the darshan
of the goddess.

name: Doleshwor Mahadev, Sipadol Bhaktapur
description:
Location, existence and description:
Doleshwor Mahadev Temple is located in Sipadol VDC of Bhaktapur
district, 20km from Kathmandu. The temple lies between the green lush
area of Sipadol. Doleshwor Mahadev is considered as a head of
Kedarnath, India. There is a legend about the link between Kedarnath
and Doleshwor Mahadev. The legend goes back to the battle of
Mahabharat between Pandavas and Kauravas brothers. The Pandavas won,
but sorrowed by the loss of lives, they renounced the kingdom they had
wrested back and headed for the heavenly absode of the gods. The
Panadavas reached the Kedarnath region to seek forgiveness from Lord
Shiva for the loss of lives during Mahabharat war. But Lord Shiva was
not ready to forgive them and he took the form of a bull to avoid
them. The Pandavas soon realized that the bull was Lord Shiva and
tried to stop it by pulling its tail. Suddenly the head got separated
from the body of the bull and they could not locate it. The
hump-backed structure at Uttarakhand's Kedarnath temple is worshipped
as the torso of the holy bull. And the head is worshipped as Doleshwor
Mahadev in Bhaktapur, Nepal. The sculptures of Shiva found in both
shrines are 4000 years old.

name: Kailashnath Mahadev Statue, Sanga
description:
Kailashnath Mahadev Temple is located in Sanga, Ward No. 5 of
Chittapol VDC, Bhaktapur district, about 20km from Kathmandu. This
statue of Lord Shiva, located on the border of Kavrepalanchok district
and Bhaktapur district, is 143 feet tall. It is currently the second
tallest statue of Lord Shiva in the world. It was constructed mainly
by Kamal Jain, an Indian citizen living in Bhatbhateni and 'Hilltake'
water tank company of Nepal. The 143-foot tall Kailashnath Mahadev
statue was installed by Badrikadham Pithadhishwar Ananta Shri
Bibhushit Shankaracharya Swami Shri Madhavashram Ji Maharaj. 100
Nepalese and Indian craftsmen were deployed from 2003 till 2011 for
completion. The statue, which is made of gravel, sand, cement, and
rods, has been zinc coated and sprayed with copper to protect it from
the sun and water. It is said that 6,000 kilograms of copper and zinc
were used for that. The statue's foundation is about 100ft deep, which
was necessary to anchor the structure into the ridge. Alcohol and
smoking are prohibited in this temple area, which is built on an area
of ​​more than 75 ropanis.

name: Nagarkot
description:
Nagarkot is a former VDC located 32km northeast of Kathmandu and 20km
east of Bhaktapur city, Nepal in Bhaktapur district. It is located
approximately 2000m above sea level and 28 km from Tribhuwan Intl
Airport. At an elevation of 2195m, it is considered one of the most
scenic spots in Bhaktapur district. It is known for a sunrise view of
the Himalayan ranges. Nagarkot commands one of the broadest views of 8
Himalayan ranges which include Annapurna range, Manaslu range, Ganesh
Himal range, Langtang range, Jugal range, Rolwaling range, Mahalangur
range (Everest range) and Numbur range with views of the Kathmandu
valley and Shivapuri National Park.
The scenery of the place makes it a popular hiking route for tourists.
There are plenty of simple, middle and high class hotels and resorts
for stay in Nagarkot. It is the place to enjoy the Himalayan vistas,
of course weather permitted, with lots of spectacular hiking trails
and beautiful nature walks. the hikes around Nagarkot will take you in
the lush green countryside of northern Nepal and deliver you stunning
mountain views, serene pine forests, peaceful villages.
